name: CHEM 1A Exam Review: Stoichiometry, Atomic Structure, Bonding, Gases and Equilibrium

cards.back: The amount of substance containing Avogadro's number of particles, 6.022 x 10^23. The molar mass in g/mol equals the mass of one mole of that substance.
The reactant that is used up first, so it determines the maximum amount of product. Find it by converting each reactant to moles of product and taking the smallest.
Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100%. Theoretical yield comes from stoichiometry using the limiting reactant.

cards.front: Mini-problem: How many moles are in 36.0 g of water (M = 18.0 g/mol)?
Relationship between energy, frequency and wavelength of light
cards.back: E = h*nu and c = lambda*nu, so E = h*c/lambda. h = 6.626 x 10^-34 J*s, c = 3.00 x 10^8 m/s. Shorter wavelength means higher energy.
E_n = -2.18 x 10^-18 J / n^2 (about -13.6 eV / n^2). A photon is emitted when an electron drops from higher n to lower n; its energy equals the difference.
lambda = h / (m*v). Any moving particle has wave character; it matters for tiny masses like electrons.
Position and momentum cannot both be known exactly: delta_x * delta_p >= h/(4*pi). This is why electrons are described by orbitals (probability distributions), not orbits.

cards.front: The four quantum numbers and their allowed values
cards.back: n = 1, 2, 3...; l = 0 to n-1 (s, p, d, f); m_l = -l to +l; m_s = +1/2 or -1/2. No two electrons in an atom share all four (Pauli exclusion).
In degenerate orbitals, electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins before pairing up, which minimizes electron repulsion.

cards.front: Periodic trends: atomic radius and ionization energy
cards.back: Atomic radius decreases across a period (higher effective nuclear charge) and increases down a group. Ionization energy shows the opposite trend.
The net positive charge felt by an electron after shielding by other electrons, roughly Z minus the number of core electrons. It rises across a period.
Ionic bonds form by electron transfer between atoms with a large electronegativity difference (often metal plus nonmetal). Covalent bonds share electron pairs, usually between nonmetals.

cards.front: How do you calculate formal charge?
cards.back: Formal charge = valence electrons - nonbonding electrons - (bonding electrons / 2). The best Lewis structure keeps formal charges near zero, with negative charge on the more electronegative atom.

cards.front: VSEPR: geometry of a central atom with 4 electron domains and 1 lone pair
cards.back: Electron geometry is tetrahedral; molecular geometry is trigonal pyramidal (example: NH3), bond angle a bit less than 109.5 degrees.
It has polar bonds arranged so their dipoles do not cancel. CO2 is nonpolar (linear, dipoles cancel) while H2O is polar (bent).
2 domains: sp (linear); 3 domains: sp2 (trigonal planar); 4 domains: sp3 (tetrahedral).
A single bond is one sigma bond; a double bond is one sigma plus one pi; a triple bond is one sigma plus two pi. Pi bonds form from side-on overlap of unhybridized p orbitals.

cards.front: Ideal gas law and its symbols
cards.back: PV = nRT. P = pressure, V = volume, n = moles, T = temperature in kelvin, R = 0.08206 L*atm/(mol*K) or 8.314 J/(mol*K).

cards.front: When do real gases deviate most from ideal behavior?
cards.back: At high pressure (molecule volume matters) and low temperature (attractions matter). The van der Waals equation corrects with the a (attraction) and b (volume) terms.
P_total = P_1 + P_2 + ...; each partial pressure P_i = x_i * P_total, where x_i is the mole fraction.
The enthalpy change for a reaction is the same whatever path is taken, so delta H values of steps can be added. Reversing a reaction flips the sign; multiplying it scales delta H.

cards.front: Standard enthalpy of reaction from enthalpies of formation
cards.back: delta H_rxn = sum(n * delta H_f products) - sum(n * delta H_f reactants). delta H_f of an element in its standard state is zero.
delta G = delta H - T*delta S. A reaction is spontaneous when delta G < 0. With delta H < 0 and delta S > 0 it is spontaneous at all temperatures.

cards.front: Link between delta G standard and K
cards.back: delta G standard = -R*T*ln K. If K > 1, delta G standard is negative and products are favored at equilibrium.
If Q < K the reaction shifts toward products; if Q > K it shifts toward reactants; if Q = K it is at equilibrium.

cards.front: Le Chatelier's principle: effect of adding heat to an exothermic reaction
cards.back: Heat acts like a product, so the equilibrium shifts toward reactants and K decreases. Temperature is the only change that alters the value of K.

cards.front: pH, pOH and Kw at 25 C
cards.back: pH = -log[H3O+], pOH = -log[OH-], pH + pOH = 14, and Kw = [H3O+][OH-] = 1.0 x 10^-14.
pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]). It applies to buffers; when [A-] = [HA], pH = pKa.

cards.front: Solubility product Ksp: write it for CaF2
cards.back: CaF2(s) <=> Ca2+ + 2F-, so Ksp = [Ca2+][F-]^2. If molar solubility is s, Ksp = s(2s)^2 = 4s^3.
Oxidation is loss of electrons (oxidation number rises); reduction is gain of electrons (oxidation number falls). The oxidizing agent is the species that gets reduced.
Rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, where m and n are found from experiment, not from coefficients. The overall order is m + n.
t_1/2 = 0.693 / k, independent of starting concentration. Integrated law: ln[A] = ln[A]0 - k*t.
k = A * e^(-Ea/(R*T)). Raising T or lowering activation energy Ea (as a catalyst does) increases the rate constant.

course_name: The Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs
name: COMPSCI 61A Midterm Review: Higher-Order Functions, Recursion, Objects and Interpreters

cards.back: Hiding the details of how something works behind a name or interface, so you can use it based only on what it does. Functions, data types and classes are all abstraction tools.
A function that takes another function as an argument, returns a function, or both. Examples: map, filter, and a function that builds and returns an adder.

cards.front: What does this return? def make_adder(n): return lambda x: x + n ... make_adder(3)(4)
cards.back: 7. make_adder(3) returns a function that adds 3 to its argument, and calling it with 4 gives 7.
A record of name-to-value bindings. Evaluating a name looks it up in the current frame, then each parent frame, ending at the global frame.

cards.front: Which frame is the parent of a new frame created by calling a function?
cards.back: The frame in which the function was defined (lexical scoping), not the frame from which it was called.
A function together with the environment it was defined in, so it can still access names from that enclosing frame after the outer function has returned.

cards.front: What does the nonlocal statement do?
cards.back: It lets an inner function reassign a name bound in an enclosing (non-global) function's frame instead of creating a new local binding.

cards.front: Two essential parts of a recursive function
cards.back: A base case that returns without recursing, and a recursive case that calls the function on a smaller problem moving toward the base case.

cards.front: Write factorial recursively in one line of logic
cards.back: def fact(n): return 1 if n == 0 else n * fact(n - 1). fact(4) = 4*3*2*1 = 24.
Recursion where a call makes more than one recursive call, like fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) or counting partitions. Its call structure forms a tree.
Number of ways to write n as a sum of parts up to size m = ways using at least one m (count_partitions(n-m, m)) + ways using no m (count_partitions(n, m-1)).

cards.front: Pitfall: why can naive recursive Fibonacci be slow?
cards.back: It recomputes the same subproblems many times, giving exponential time. Memoization (caching results) makes it linear.
[expression for x in iterable if condition]. Example: [x * x for x in range(5) if x % 2 == 0] gives [0, 4, 16].
An iterable can produce an iterator through iter(). An iterator returns successive values through next() and raises StopIteration when it runs out; it can be used only once.
A function containing yield. Calling it returns a generator (a lazy iterator) that runs until each yield, pausing and resuming its state between next() calls.
It yields every value from another iterable or generator in turn, which is handy for recursive generators.

cards.front: What is a data abstraction barrier?
cards.back: A separation between code that uses a data type through its constructors and selectors and code that implements its representation. Violating it means relying on internal details.

cards.front: Mutable vs immutable values in Python
cards.back: Lists and dictionaries are mutable (can change in place). Integers, strings and tuples are immutable. Two names bound to the same list both see changes made through either name.
== tests whether two values are equal. is tests identity, that is, whether both names refer to the very same object.
A class attribute is shared by all instances and stored on the class. An instance attribute is stored on one object, often set in __init__ through self.
A subclass reuses the attributes and methods of its base class and can override them. Attribute lookup checks the instance, then its class, then base classes.

cards.front: Bound method: what happens with obj.method(arg)?
cards.back: Python looks up method on the class and passes obj automatically as the first parameter, self, so it is the same as Class.method(obj, arg).
__str__ gives a readable string used by print and str(). __repr__ gives an unambiguous string, ideally valid code, shown by the interactive interpreter and repr().
A recursive sequence where each node holds a first value and a rest, which is another linked list or empty. Access to the k-th element takes time proportional to k.

cards.front: What is a tree in 61A-style data abstraction?
cards.back: A value with a label and a list of branches, where each branch is itself a tree. A leaf has no branches.

cards.front: Order of growth: what is Theta(log n)?
cards.back: Time grows with the logarithm of input size, typical when each step halves the problem, as in binary search or repeated halving of n.

cards.front: Order of growth of a nested loop over n items for each of n items
cards.back: Theta(n^2), quadratic: doubling n roughly quadruples the work.

cards.front: Functional vs object-oriented vs declarative paradigms
cards.back: Functional: compose pure functions and avoid mutation. Object-oriented: bundle state and behavior in objects. Declarative: state what result you want (as in SQL) rather than how to compute it.

cards.front: In Scheme, what does (define (square x) (* x x)) do?
cards.back: It binds the name square to a procedure that multiplies its argument by itself. Scheme uses prefix notation with the operator first inside parentheses.

cards.front: What are the two core steps of an interpreter's eval loop?
cards.back: Eval evaluates an expression: for a call it evaluates the operator and operands. Apply then calls the procedure on those argument values, often by evaluating its body in a new frame.

cards.front: Special form vs call expression in Scheme
cards.back: A call expression evaluates all operands first. Special forms such as if, define, lambda and and do not evaluate all subexpressions in the usual way.
A procedure that operates on unevaluated code and returns new code, which is then evaluated in the caller's environment. It lets you add new special forms to a language.

cards.front: What is tail recursion and why does it matter in Scheme?
cards.back: A call is in tail position when nothing remains to do after it returns. Scheme implementations must optimize tail calls, so tail-recursive procedures use constant space.

name: ECON 1 Final Review: Supply and Demand, Market Structures, GDP and Macro Policy

cards.back: The value of the next best alternative given up when you make a choice. For example, the cost of college includes wages you could have earned.
Absolute advantage: producing more with the same resources. Comparative advantage: producing at a lower opportunity cost. Trade gains come from comparative advantage.

cards.front: What does a production possibilities frontier (PPF) show?
cards.back: The maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its resources. Points inside are inefficient, points outside unattainable; a bowed-out shape reflects increasing opportunity cost.
Other things equal, when the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, so demand curves slope downward.

cards.front: Change in demand vs change in quantity demanded
cards.back: A price change moves you along the demand curve (quantity demanded). A change in income, tastes, related goods' prices, expectations or number of buyers shifts the whole curve (demand).
Demand for a normal good rises when income rises. Demand for an inferior good falls when income rises.
Substitutes: a price rise in one raises demand for the other (coffee and tea). Complements: a price rise in one lowers demand for the other (cars and gasoline).

cards.front: Effect of a supply decrease on equilibrium
cards.back: Supply shifts left: equilibrium price rises and equilibrium quantity falls.
Elasticity = (% change in quantity demanded) / (% change in price), in absolute value. Greater than 1 is elastic, less than 1 is inelastic.

cards.front: How does a price increase affect total revenue for inelastic demand?
cards.back: Total revenue rises, because quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises. For elastic demand, revenue falls.
Consumer surplus: willingness to pay minus price paid (area under demand above price). Producer surplus: price received minus cost (area above supply below price).
The loss of total surplus when output is not at the efficient level, for example from a tax, price ceiling, price floor or monopoly.

cards.front: Effect of a binding price ceiling
cards.back: Set below equilibrium, it causes a shortage: quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. Rent control is a standard example.
The side of the market that is less elastic bears more of a tax burden, regardless of whether the tax is legally placed on buyers or sellers.

cards.front: Marginal cost and average total cost relationship
cards.back: MC crosses ATC at the minimum point of ATC. When MC is below ATC, ATC is falling; when MC is above ATC, ATC is rising.
Produce the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost (MR = MC).

cards.front: Perfect competition in the long run
cards.back: Free entry and exit drive economic profit to zero, so price equals minimum average total cost and P = MC.

cards.front: How does a monopoly differ from a competitive firm?
cards.back: A monopolist faces the downward-sloping market demand, so MR < P. It sets MR = MC, producing less and charging more than a competitive market, creating deadweight loss.

cards.front: What is a negative externality and one fix?
cards.back: A cost imposed on third parties not reflected in price, such as pollution, leading to overproduction. A Pigouvian tax equal to the external cost can correct it.
Non-rival (one person's use does not reduce another's) and non-excludable (people cannot be kept from using it). They suffer from the free-rider problem.
GDP = C + I + G + NX: consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports (exports minus imports).
Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP uses constant base-year prices, so it measures changes in output alone. GDP deflator = (nominal / real) x 100.

cards.front: Unemployment rate formula and who counts
cards.back: Unemployment rate = unemployed / labor force x 100. The labor force is employed plus unemployed people actively seeking work; discouraged workers are excluded.
Frictional (between jobs), structural (skill or location mismatch), and cyclical (due to recessions). The natural rate includes frictional and structural only.

cards.front: Mini-problem: CPI rises from 200 to 210. What is the inflation rate?

cards.back: Real interest rate is approximately nominal interest rate minus inflation. A 7% nominal rate with 3% inflation gives about a 4% real rate.
Multiplier = 1 / (1 - MPC), where MPC is the marginal propensity to consume. With MPC = 0.8, a change in spending is multiplied by 5.

cards.front: Aggregate demand and aggregate supply: effect of a negative demand shock in the short run
cards.back: AD shifts left: output falls, unemployment rises and the price level falls or rises more slowly.

cards.front: Expansionary fiscal policy vs expansionary monetary policy
cards.back: Fiscal: the government raises spending or cuts taxes. Monetary: the central bank lowers interest rates or expands the money supply. Both shift aggregate demand right.
M*V = P*Y: money supply times velocity equals the price level times real output. With stable V and Y, faster money growth leads to inflation.

name: PSYC 100 Exam Review: Research Methods, Brain, Learning, Memory and Disorders

cards.back: A correlational study measures how variables relate without manipulating them, so it cannot show cause. An experiment manipulates an independent variable and uses random assignment to infer causation.
The independent variable is what the researcher manipulates. The dependent variable is the outcome that is measured.
It spreads participant differences evenly across conditions, so differences in the outcome can be attributed to the manipulation rather than preexisting differences.
Neither participants nor the researchers interacting with them know who is in which condition, reducing placebo effects and experimenter bias.
Reliability is consistency of a measure across time or raters. Validity is whether it measures what it claims to measure. A measure can be reliable without being valid.

cards.front: Parts of a neuron and the direction of signal flow
cards.back: Dendrites receive signals, the cell body integrates them, and the axon carries the action potential to the terminals, which release neurotransmitters into the synapse.
An all-or-none electrical impulse along the axon, triggered when the membrane reaches threshold; sodium ions rush in, then potassium flows out to restore the charge.
Dopamine is involved in reward, motivation and movement (low in Parkinson's). Serotonin is involved in mood, sleep and appetite (targeted by SSRIs for depression).

cards.front: Functions of the frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes
cards.back: Frontal: planning, decisions, motor control. Parietal: touch and spatial processing. Temporal: hearing and language comprehension. Occipital: vision.
Damage to Broca's area (frontal) impairs speech production. Damage to Wernicke's area (temporal) impairs language comprehension, with fluent but meaningless speech.

cards.front: Role of the hippocampus and amygdala
cards.back: The hippocampus helps form new explicit memories. The amygdala processes emotion, especially fear.
Sensation is detecting physical energy with sense receptors. Perception is the brain organizing and interpreting that input into meaningful experience.

cards.front: Classical conditioning terms in Pavlov's experiment
cards.back: Food is the unconditioned stimulus, salivation to food the unconditioned response. The bell becomes a conditioned stimulus, and salivation to the bell the conditioned response.

cards.front: What is extinction in classical conditioning?
cards.back: The conditioned response weakens when the conditioned stimulus is repeatedly presented without the unconditioned stimulus. It can return later (spontaneous recovery).
Both increase a behavior. Positive reinforcement adds something pleasant; negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant, like taking aspirin to remove a headache.
Negative reinforcement increases behavior by removing an aversive stimulus. Punishment decreases behavior. They are often confused.

cards.front: Which reinforcement schedule is most resistant to extinction?
cards.back: Variable-ratio, where reward comes after an unpredictable number of responses (like a slot machine).

cards.front: Bandura's Bobo doll study showed what?
cards.back: Children who watched an adult act aggressively toward a doll imitated that aggression, demonstrating observational learning.

cards.front: Stages of the multi-store (Atkinson-Shiffrin) memory model
cards.back: Sensory memory, then short-term (working) memory with limited capacity, then long-term memory. Attention moves information to short-term memory; encoding moves it to long-term.
Explicit (declarative) memory is consciously recalled facts and events. Implicit memory includes skills and conditioned responses shown without conscious recall, like riding a bike.
Proactive: old learning disrupts recall of new information. Retroactive: new learning disrupts recall of old information.

cards.front: Piaget's four stages of cognitive development
cards.back: Sensorimotor (0-2, object permanence), preoperational (2-7, egocentrism), concrete operational (7-11, conservation), and formal operational (12+, abstract reasoning).

cards.front: Ainsworth's Strange Situation identified which attachment styles?
cards.back: Secure, insecure-avoidant and insecure-resistant (ambivalent); later work added disorganized attachment.
Openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism (OCEAN).
Overestimating personal traits and underestimating situational factors when explaining other people's behavior.

cards.front: What did Milgram's obedience study find?
cards.back: Most participants obeyed an authority figure's instructions to give what they believed were severe electric shocks, showing the strong power of situational authority.
Discomfort from holding conflicting beliefs or acting against one's beliefs, which people often reduce by changing their attitudes.

cards.front: Major depressive disorder vs bipolar disorder
cards.back: Major depression involves persistent low mood or loss of interest. Bipolar disorder involves depressive episodes plus manic or hypomanic episodes.
Positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions, disorganized speech, and negative symptoms such as flat affect and reduced motivation.

cards.front: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) in one sentence
cards.back: A therapy that helps people identify and change distorted thoughts and maladaptive behaviors; it is well supported for depression and anxiety.

cards.front: Stages of sleep and when vivid dreaming mostly occurs
cards.back: Sleep cycles through NREM stages 1-3 (stage 3 is deep slow-wave sleep) and REM sleep, about every 90 minutes. Vivid dreams occur mostly in REM.

name: BUAD 280 Midterm Review: Accounting Equation, Financial Statements, Inventory and Receivables

cards.back: Assets = Liabilities + Stockholders' Equity. Every transaction keeps it in balance.
Equity = Common Stock (contributed capital) + Retained Earnings. Retained earnings rise with net income and fall with net losses and dividends.

cards.front: Debit and credit rules for the five account types
cards.back: Assets, expenses and dividends increase with debits. Liabilities, equity and revenues increase with credits.

cards.front: What are the four main financial statements?
cards.back: Income statement, statement of retained earnings (or stockholders' equity), balance sheet, and statement of cash flows.
The income statement reports revenues and expenses over a period. The balance sheet reports assets, liabilities and equity at a single point in time.

cards.front: Order in which the statements are prepared and why
cards.back: Income statement first (net income), then retained earnings (uses net income), then balance sheet (uses ending retained earnings), then cash flows.
Accrual accounting records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of cash. Cash basis records them when cash changes hands. GAAP requires accrual.
Recognize revenue when the company satisfies its performance obligation by transferring goods or services to the customer, in the amount it expects to receive.
Record expenses in the same period as the revenues they helped generate.

cards.front: Journal entry: company receives $5,000 cash for services to be performed next month
cards.back: Debit Cash 5,000; credit Unearned Revenue 5,000. Unearned revenue is a liability until the service is performed.
Deferred revenues (unearned revenue earned), deferred expenses (prepaids used up), accrued revenues (earned but not billed) and accrued expenses (incurred but not paid).

cards.front: Adjusting entry: $1,200 of prepaid insurance covers 12 months; one month has passed
cards.back: Debit Insurance Expense 100; credit Prepaid Insurance 100.
Allocating the cost of a long-term asset over its useful life. It is a cost allocation, not a measure of market value. Entry: debit Depreciation Expense, credit Accumulated Depreciation.
(Cost - Residual value) / Useful life. A $10,000 asset with $1,000 residual value and 3-year life gives $3,000 per year.

cards.front: What is a contra account? Give an example
cards.back: An account offsetting a related account, with the opposite normal balance. Accumulated Depreciation reduces equipment; Allowance for Doubtful Accounts reduces receivables.

cards.front: Which accounts are closed at period end?
cards.back: Temporary accounts: revenues, expenses and dividends are closed to Retained Earnings. Permanent balance sheet accounts carry forward.
Gross profit = Net sales - Cost of goods sold. Gross profit percentage = gross profit / net sales.
COGS = Beginning inventory + Purchases - Ending inventory.

cards.front: FIFO vs LIFO when costs are rising
cards.back: FIFO assigns older, cheaper costs to COGS, giving higher net income and higher ending inventory. LIFO gives higher COGS, lower income and lower taxes. IFRS does not allow LIFO.
Perpetual updates inventory and COGS with each sale. Periodic updates them only at the end of the period through a physical count.

cards.front: Lower of cost and net realizable value rule
cards.back: If inventory's net realizable value falls below cost, write it down to NRV, recognizing a loss in that period.
Estimate uncollectible accounts each period: debit Bad Debt Expense, credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts. A write-off later debits the Allowance and credits Accounts Receivable, with no expense.

cards.front: Net realizable value of accounts receivable
cards.back: Accounts Receivable minus Allowance for Doubtful Accounts: the amount the company expects to collect.

cards.front: Three sections of the statement of cash flows
cards.back: Operating activities (core business), investing activities (buying or selling long-term assets and investments) and financing activities (debt, stock, dividends).

cards.front: Under the indirect method, how is depreciation treated?
cards.back: It is added back to net income in operating activities, because it reduced net income without using cash.
Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities. It measures short-term liquidity; above 1 means current assets exceed current obligations.
Total liabilities / total stockholders' equity. A higher ratio means more financing comes from creditors and more financial risk.
Net income / average total assets. It measures how efficiently a company uses its assets to generate profit.

cards.front: Effect of declaring a cash dividend
cards.back: Retained earnings decrease and a dividends payable liability is created. Dividends are not an expense and do not appear on the income statement.

cards.front: Mini-problem: Assets $80,000 and liabilities $30,000. What is equity?
cards.back: Equity = Assets - Liabilities = 80,000 - 30,000 = $50,000.

name: MATH 125 Final Review: Limits, Derivatives, Applications and the Fundamental Theorem

cards.front: Informal meaning of lim x->a f(x) = L
cards.back: f(x) can be made as close to L as we like by taking x close enough to a, but not equal to a. The value f(a) itself does not matter.

cards.front: When does a limit fail to exist?
cards.back: When the left and right limits differ, when f grows without bound, or when f oscillates without settling, as sin(1/x) does near 0.
Factor: (x - 3)(x + 3)/(x - 3) = x + 3, so the limit is 6.
lim x->0 sin(x)/x = 1. Also lim x->0 (1 - cos x)/x = 0.

cards.front: Three conditions for continuity at x = a
cards.back: f(a) is defined, lim x->a f(x) exists, and the limit equals f(a).
If f is continuous on [a, b] and N is between f(a) and f(b), then f(c) = N for some c in [a, b]. Used to show a root exists.
f'(x) = lim h->0 [f(x + h) - f(x)] / h: the slope of the tangent line, or instantaneous rate of change.

cards.front: Pitfall: does differentiable imply continuous, and vice versa?
cards.back: Differentiable implies continuous, but continuous does not imply differentiable. |x| is continuous at 0 but has a corner there.
d/dx [x^n] = n*x^(n-1) for any real n. Example: d/dx [x^(1/2)] = (1/2)x^(-1/2).
d/dx [f*g] = f'*g + f*g'.
d/dx [f(g(x))] = f'(g(x)) * g'(x). Example: d/dx [sin(x^2)] = cos(x^2) * 2x.

cards.front: Derivatives of sin x, cos x and tan x
cards.back: d/dx sin x = cos x; d/dx cos x = -sin x; d/dx tan x = sec^2 x.

cards.front: Derivatives of e^x and ln x
cards.back: d/dx e^x = e^x; d/dx ln x = 1/x for x > 0. Also d/dx a^x = a^x * ln a.

cards.front: Implicit differentiation: find dy/dx for x^2 + y^2 = 25
cards.back: 2x + 2y*(dy/dx) = 0, so dy/dx = -x/y.
Write an equation linking the quantities, differentiate both sides with respect to time t, then substitute known values only after differentiating.

cards.front: Equation of the tangent line at x = a
cards.back: y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a). This is also the linear approximation of f near a.
A number c in the domain where f'(c) = 0 or f'(c) does not exist. Local extrema can occur only at critical numbers.
If f' changes from positive to negative at c, f has a local max there; negative to positive gives a local min; no sign change gives neither.
f'' > 0 means concave up; f'' < 0 means concave down. If f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) > 0, then c is a local min; if f''(c) < 0, a local max.
A point on the graph where concavity changes, from up to down or down to up.
If f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then f'(c) = [f(b) - f(a)] / (b - a) for some c in (a, b).

cards.front: Closed interval method for absolute extrema
cards.back: Evaluate f at critical numbers in [a, b] and at endpoints a and b. The largest value is the absolute max; the smallest is the absolute min.
If a limit gives 0/0 or infinity/infinity, then lim f/g = lim f'/g' when the latter exists. Example: lim x->0 sin x / x = lim cos x / 1 = 1.
Integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n not equal to -1. For n = -1 it is ln|x| + C.

cards.front: Why is + C needed in an indefinite integral?
cards.back: Any two antiderivatives of the same function differ by a constant, so C represents the whole family.

cards.front: Definite integral as a Riemann sum
cards.back: Integral from a to b of f(x) dx = limit as n -> infinity of the sum of f(x_i)*delta_x, with delta_x = (b - a)/n. It is signed area under the curve.
If F(x) = integral from a to x of f(t) dt with f continuous, then F'(x) = f(x).
Integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a), where F is any antiderivative of f.

cards.front: Evaluate the integral from 0 to 2 of 3x^2 dx
cards.back: Antiderivative x^3; 2^3 - 0^3 = 8.
Let u = x^2, du = 2x dx, so the integral is integral of cos u du = sin(x^2) + C.

name: BIOL 180 Exam Review: Mendelian Genetics, Evolution, Biodiversity and Ecology

cards.back: Each individual has two alleles for a gene, which separate during gamete formation so each gamete carries only one.
Alleles of different genes assort into gametes independently of one another, as long as the genes are on different chromosomes or far apart on the same one.
Genotype is the allele combination an organism carries. Phenotype is its observable trait, which results from genotype and environment.

cards.front: Expected ratios from a monohybrid cross Aa x Aa
cards.back: Genotypes 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa; phenotypes 3 dominant : 1 recessive.

cards.front: Expected phenotype ratio from a dihybrid cross AaBb x AaBb
cards.back: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, assuming complete dominance and independent assortment.
Crossing an individual with the dominant phenotype to a homozygous recessive. If any offspring show the recessive phenotype, the parent was heterozygous.
Incomplete dominance: heterozygote is intermediate (red x white gives pink). Codominance: both alleles fully expressed (AB blood type).

cards.front: Why are X-linked recessive traits more common in males?
cards.back: Males have one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele produces the trait; females need two copies.

cards.front: How does meiosis create genetic variation?
cards.back: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes in prophase I, independent assortment of homologs in metaphase I, and random fertilization.
Mitosis gives two genetically identical diploid cells. Meiosis gives four genetically different haploid gametes.
Genes close on a chromosome tend to be inherited together. Recombination frequency (recombinant offspring / total) estimates distance: 1% = 1 map unit.

cards.front: Darwin's natural selection in four points
cards.back: Individuals vary, variation is heritable, more offspring are produced than survive, and individuals with advantageous traits leave more offspring, so those traits increase over generations.
An individual's relative reproductive success: how many offspring it contributes to the next generation compared with others.
p + q = 1 for allele frequencies and p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1 for genotype frequencies (AA, Aa, aa).
No mutation, random mating, no natural selection, very large population (no drift) and no gene flow.

cards.front: Mini-problem: 16% of a population shows a recessive trait. What is q?
cards.back: q^2 = 0.16, so q = 0.4 and p = 0.6. Heterozygotes are 2pq = 0.48.

cards.front: Genetic drift, and the bottleneck vs founder effect
cards.back: Drift is random change in allele frequencies, strongest in small populations. Bottleneck: a population sharply shrinks. Founder effect: a few individuals start a new population.
Directional favors one extreme; stabilizing favors intermediate phenotypes; disruptive favors both extremes over the middle.
A species is a group of populations whose members can interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring, and are reproductively isolated from other groups.
Allopatric: populations are separated geographically and diverge. Sympatric: new species arise in the same area, for example through polyploidy in plants.
Homologous structures share common ancestry (human arm and whale flipper). Analogous structures have similar function from convergent evolution (bird and insect wings).
An ancestor and all of its descendants. Paraphyletic groups leave out some descendants, such as traditional reptiles without birds.
Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Bacteria and Archaea are prokaryotes; Archaea share some molecular features with eukaryotes.
Exponential: dN/dt = rN, a J-shaped curve with unlimited resources. Logistic: dN/dt = rN(K - N)/K, an S-shaped curve leveling off at carrying capacity K.
r-selected: many offspring, little care, fast maturity (often in unstable habitats). K-selected: few offspring, high parental care, near carrying capacity.

cards.front: Types of species interactions with their +/- effects
cards.back: Competition (-/-), predation and parasitism (+/-), mutualism (+/+), commensalism (+/0).
Two species competing for the exact same limiting resources cannot coexist indefinitely; one will outcompete the other or they will partition resources.
A species whose effect on community structure is far larger than its abundance suggests, like sea otters controlling urchins and protecting kelp forests.

cards.front: Why is only about 10% of energy passed between trophic levels?
cards.back: Most energy is lost as heat in metabolism or remains in unconsumed or undigested material, which limits the length of food chains.
Habitat loss and fragmentation, invasive species, overharvesting, pollution and climate change.

cards.front: Why does small population size threaten conservation?
cards.back: Small populations lose genetic diversity through drift and inbreeding, lowering fitness and adaptability, which can create an extinction vortex.

name: STAT 311 Final Review: Study Design, Probability, Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Tests

cards.back: An observational study records data without assigning treatments, so it shows association only. An experiment randomly assigns treatments, allowing cause-and-effect conclusions.
A variable related to both the explanatory variable and the response, making it impossible to separate their effects.

cards.front: Simple random sample vs stratified sample
cards.back: SRS: every group of n individuals is equally likely to be chosen. Stratified: divide the population into similar groups (strata) and take an SRS within each.
Control (comparison groups and holding variables constant), randomization, and replication (enough units). Blocking can also reduce variability.

cards.front: Mean vs median with a skewed distribution
cards.back: The mean is pulled toward the tail; the median is resistant. In right-skewed data the mean is usually greater than the median.

cards.front: Interquartile range and the 1.5 x IQR outlier rule
cards.back: IQR = Q3 - Q1. Values below Q1 - 1.5*IQR or above Q3 + 1.5*IQR are flagged as potential outliers.
Roughly the typical distance of observations from the mean. Sample formula: s = sqrt(sum((x - xbar)^2) / (n - 1)).
r ranges from -1 to 1 and measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship. It has no units, is unaffected by changes of scale, and is sensitive to outliers.
y-hat = b0 + b1*x, with slope b1 = r * (s_y / s_x) and intercept b0 = ybar - b1*xbar.
The proportion of variation in y explained by the linear relationship with x. r^2 = 0.64 means 64% of the variation is explained.
Residual = observed y - predicted y-hat. A residual plot with no pattern supports a linear model.
Using a regression line to predict far outside the range of observed x values, which is unreliable because the relationship may not continue.
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). For disjoint events, P(A and B) = 0.
P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B). A and B are independent if P(A | B) = P(A), equivalently P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B).
Fixed number of trials n, each trial success or failure, trials independent, and the same success probability p on each trial.
Mean = n*p; SD = sqrt(n*p*(1 - p)). With n = 100 and p = 0.3, the mean is 30 and SD is about 4.58.
In a normal distribution about 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean, 95% within 2 SD, and 99.7% within 3 SD.
z = (x - mu) / sigma: how many standard deviations x is above or below the mean.
For large n, the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal with mean mu and standard deviation sigma / sqrt(n), whatever the population shape.

cards.front: Standard error of a sample proportion
cards.back: SE = sqrt(p-hat * (1 - p-hat) / n). For a test, use the null value p0 in place of p-hat.

cards.front: General form of a confidence interval
cards.back: Estimate plus or minus (critical value x standard error). For a mean: xbar plus or minus t* * s / sqrt(n).

cards.front: Correct interpretation of a 95% confidence interval
cards.back: If we repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of the intervals built this way would contain the true parameter. It is not a 95% chance this one interval contains it.

cards.front: How do sample size and confidence level affect interval width?
cards.back: Larger n gives a narrower interval (SE shrinks with sqrt(n)). Higher confidence gives a wider interval.
Assuming the null hypothesis is true, the probability of getting a result at least as extreme as the one observed. Small p-values are evidence against H0.

cards.front: Type I vs Type II error
cards.back: Type I: rejecting a true null hypothesis (probability alpha). Type II: failing to reject a false null hypothesis (probability beta). Power = 1 - beta.
t = (xbar - mu0) / (s / sqrt(n)), with n - 1 degrees of freedom. Used when the population SD is unknown.
Paired: the same subjects measured twice or matched pairs, so analyze the differences. Two-sample: two independent groups, compare their means.
Chi-square = sum of (observed - expected)^2 / expected over all cells. Large values indicate the data differ from what H0 predicts.

cards.front: Expected count in a chi-square test of independence
cards.back: Expected = (row total x column total) / grand total. Each expected count should be at least about 5.

cards.front: Mini-problem: n = 25, xbar = 52, s = 10, testing mu0 = 50. Find t.
cards.back: SE = 10 / sqrt(25) = 2, so t = (52 - 50) / 2 = 1.0 with 24 degrees of freedom.
With a very large sample, even a tiny, unimportant difference can give a small p-value. Always consider the size of the effect, for example through a confidence interval.

name: PHYS 121 Exam Review: Kinematics, Newton's Laws, Energy, Momentum and Rotation

cards.back: Displacement is the vector change in position (final minus initial). Distance is the total path length, a scalar that is never negative.
Average velocity = displacement / elapsed time. Instantaneous velocity is the derivative dx/dt, the slope of the position-time graph at an instant.

cards.front: Mini-problem: A ball is dropped from rest. How far does it fall in 2.0 s? (g = 9.8 m/s^2)

cards.back: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Horizontal velocity is constant (no air resistance); vertical acceleration is -g.

cards.front: Range of a projectile launched and landing at the same height
cards.back: R = v0^2 * sin(2*theta) / g, which is greatest at 45 degrees.
Centripetal acceleration a = v^2 / r, directed toward the center, even at constant speed.
An object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a net external force acts on it (inertia).
F_net = m*a, where F_net is the vector sum of all forces, m is mass in kg and a is acceleration in m/s^2.

cards.front: Newton's third law and a common pitfall
cards.back: Forces come in equal and opposite pairs acting on different objects. The normal force and weight on a resting book are not a third-law pair; both act on the book.
Mass is the amount of matter (kg), the same everywhere. Weight is the gravitational force on it, W = m*g, measured in newtons.
Static friction adjusts up to a maximum f_s <= mu_s*N to prevent sliding. Kinetic friction f_k = mu_k*N acts during sliding. Usually mu_k < mu_s.

cards.front: Block on a frictionless incline at angle theta: acceleration?
cards.back: a = g*sin(theta) down the slope; the normal force is m*g*cos(theta).

cards.front: Atwood machine: two masses m1 > m2 over a frictionless pulley. Acceleration?
Work done by a constant force
cards.back: W = F*d*cos(theta), where theta is the angle between force and displacement. Units: joules (N*m).
The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = delta KE, with KE = (1/2)*m*v^2.
Near Earth, U_g = m*g*h. For a spring, U_s = (1/2)*k*x^2, where k is the spring constant and x the stretch or compression.
With only conservative forces doing work, KE + U is constant. Friction converts mechanical energy into thermal energy.

cards.front: Mini-problem: speed at the bottom of a frictionless 5.0 m drop starting from rest?
cards.back: v = sqrt(2*g*h) = sqrt(2 * 9.8 * 5.0), which is about 9.9 m/s.
P = W / t = F*v, the rate of doing work, measured in watts (J/s).
Momentum p = m*v. Impulse J = F_avg * delta_t = delta p.
When the net external force on the system is zero; internal forces in a collision do not change total momentum.
Both conserve momentum. Elastic collisions also conserve kinetic energy. In a perfectly inelastic collision the objects stick together and the most kinetic energy is lost.

cards.front: Mini-problem: 2 kg cart at 3 m/s sticks to a resting 1 kg cart. Final speed?
cards.back: Momentum conservation: 2*3 = (2 + 1)*v, so v = 2 m/s.

cards.front: Center of mass of a system of particles
cards.back: x_cm = sum(m_i * x_i) / sum(m_i). With no net external force, the center of mass moves at constant velocity.

cards.front: Rotational kinematics links between linear and angular quantities
cards.back: s = r*theta, v = r*omega, a_tangential = r*alpha, with angles in radians.
tau = r*F*sin(theta), the rotational effect of a force about an axis. Newton's second law for rotation: tau_net = I*alpha.

cards.front: Moment of inertia and why it depends on shape
cards.back: I = sum(m_i * r_i^2): rotational inertia depends on how far mass sits from the axis. A hoop (I = M*R^2) is harder to spin than a solid disk (I = (1/2)*M*R^2).

cards.front: Rotational kinetic energy and rolling without slipping
cards.back: KE_rot = (1/2)*I*omega^2. For rolling without slipping v = R*omega and total KE = (1/2)*m*v^2 + (1/2)*I*omega^2.
L = I*omega is constant when net external torque is zero. A skater pulling in her arms lowers I, so omega increases.
Net force is zero and net torque about any axis is zero.

cards.front: Hooke's law and simple harmonic motion period
cards.back: F = -k*x. A mass on a spring oscillates with period T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k), independent of amplitude.
